title: ⭐⭐ Revision: from the launch pad to the dictionary

questions.prompt: How many words in this sentence contain the sound [ei], the vowel of "space"? — "They came late to the gate and missed the flight."
questions.explanation: The count is 4: they, came, late and gate all carry it. The sound hides behind several spellings — a…e in came, late and gate, -ai- in paid, -ay- in delay, and even -ea- in the two odd words great and break — while they belongs to no pattern at all and has to be learnt on its own. The trap here is flight, where letters that look very much like the a…e of late give [ai] instead, the vowel of price and mile. Never trust the letters alone: say the word aloud and listen for the vowel that ends like the letter y in say.

questions.prompt: An article speaks of "the emerging space-tourism industry". What does "emerging" mean here?

options.text: coming to an end
joining two companies together
extremely wealthy
beginning to be known

questions.explanation: An emerging industry is one that is appearing and starting to be known: it exists, but the public is only just discovering it. The word comes from to emerge, to come out into view, so it always points to a beginning and never to an end. The idea of joining two things together belongs to merge, which is one letter away, and wealth belongs to well-to-do, another word of this lesson.

questions.prompt: A student wrote: "At the meeting the chief engineer suggested to delay the launch by a week." What must be changed?

options.text: "suggested" must become "suggested that".
"to delay" must become "delaying".
"to delay" must become "delay".
Nothing — the sentence is already correct.

questions.explanation: When suggest is followed straight by a verb, that verb wears the -ing form and no other: the engineer suggested delaying the launch. "Suggested to delay" is the mistake nearly every learner makes, because in many languages the idea of proposing something is followed by an infinitive. Dropping the to would leave two verbs touching with nothing between them, and "suggested that" opens a whole clause behind it — suggested that we delay the launch — which is another sentence altogether, not a repair of this one.

questions.prompt: You want to say that the guide interrupted the tour in order to answer a phone call. Which sentence says exactly that?

options.text: The guide stopped answering a phone call.
The guide stopped for answering a phone call.
The guide stopped to answer a phone call.
The guide stopped answering to a phone call.

questions.explanation: Only to + infinitive gives the purpose of the interruption: he stopped in order to answer. "Stopped answering" says the opposite — that he had been answering calls and gave that up. "Stopped for answering" borrows a preposition from other languages where English uses to on its own, and to answer to somebody means to be responsible to that person, not to pick up a telephone.

questions.prompt: A spaceport notice reads: "Non-paying visitors must stay outside the launch area." Why does English write non- here and not un-?

options.text: Non- puts the visitor outside the group that pays; un- would say the reverse of paying.
Non- is the form that English always uses whenever the word after it wears the -ing ending.
Non- is the American spelling of this prefix, and un- is the British spelling of it.
Non- is chosen because the word that follows it begins with a consonant sound.

questions.explanation: Non- states an absence, not an opposite: a non-paying visitor is simply somebody standing outside the group who bought a ticket, exactly as a non-smoker is nobody's enemy and only somebody who does not smoke. Un- would try to say the reverse of paying, and that means nothing here. Nor is the choice made by the letter that follows — that rule belongs to il-, im- and ir-; neither spelling belongs to one side of the Atlantic; and non- sits just as comfortably in front of an ordinary adjective, as in non-violent.

questions.prompt: A dictionary gives: "foothold (noun) — a first strong position from which you can make progress". Which sentence uses the word as the entry describes it?

options.text: He built a foothold next to the spaceport.
The foothold of the rocket burned on re-entry.
He hung his coat on a foothold by the door.
The company has gained a foothold in China.

questions.explanation: The entry defines a position, not an object: you gain, get or win a foothold, and what you gain is the right to go further — here a first place in the Chinese market from which the company can grow. A position of that kind cannot be built next to a building, cannot burn on re-entry and is certainly not a hook you hang a coat on. The first words of a definition tell you what kind of word you are holding, and "a position" already rules three of these sentences out.
